title: Shema Yisrael
description: The Shema, the line from Deuteronomy at the heart of every Jewish service, to the familiar congregational tune of Reform and Conservative synagogues, known as Sulzer's, for 2 to 4 singers. "Hear, Israel: Hashem is ours, Hashem is one", then Baruch shem, "Blessed be the name of His glorious kingdom for ever and ever", which the tune's earliest known printing, of 1926, adds for Yom Kippur. Slow and broad, sung in Hebrew.

credits.words: Deuteronomy 6:4 and the traditional response (Baruch shem)
credits.tune: traditional, known as "Sulzer's" Shema, probably by Jacob Beimel, as printed in 1926

licence.words: public domain: the Hebrew Bible (Deuteronomy 6:4) and the traditional response of the liturgy
licence.tune: public domain: printed in the United States in 1926 (before 1931); the page calls it "Traditional". Known as Sulzer's Shema, but it is not the Shema Salomon Sulzer (died 1890) printed in Schir Zion (vol. 1, No. 104 in Joseph Sulzer's revised edition), which shares only its meter, its first note and its closing "Adoshem echad". Geoffrey Goldberg (Journal of Synagogue Music, 2019) argues it should be attributed to the cantor Jacob Beimel (died 1944), whose manuscript shows it taking shape, and calls this 1926 page its first printed occurrence. The 1926 book, compiled by Israel Goldfarb (died 1967) and Samuel E. Goldfarb (died 1978), is melody only throughout, one line for cantor or congregation with no harmony, and marks its own work by name ("I. Goldfarb" on No. 8, "Adapted by I. Goldfarb" on No. 26); this Shema it marks "Traditional", so nothing of theirs is in what we sing, and they are credited as its earliest known printing, not as makers.
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella under the printed tune (the print is one unison line for the congregation): the alto mostly a third or a sixth under the tune, the tenor and bass our own (G, E minor 7, C, A minor 7, G over D, D at the half close on "Elokeinu"; G over D, D7, G at "Adoshem echad"). Accepted exceptions (singable.py and the app's check): in Baruch shem the alto slurs G to F-sharp on "to", in thirds under the tune's own B to A on that syllable, where a single held note would clash or leave a bare fourth on the downbeat; at the A minor 7 on "E-lo-" and "mal-chu-" (two eighths) and the D7 on "e-" and "va-" the third is in the tenor only, so 2 and 3 singers hear those chords without it: the alto there sings D, C, B in sixths under the tune's B, A, G, into a complete last chord.
licence.source: Israel Goldfarb and Samuel E. Goldfarb, Synagogue Melodies for the High Holy Days (Shirim l'Yamim Nora'im), "arranged for congregational singing" (Brooklyn, N.Y., 5686, 1926), No. 18, "Sh'ma Yisroel", and No. 19, "Boruch Shem" ("On Yom Kippur add"), p. 17: one line for the congregation ("Cong."), G major, 3/4, no tempo mark, "Traditional", with "Boruch shem" as a second verse under the same six bars, marked "For Yom Kippur". Written here in G as printed, at 72 (it is printed with fermatas and sung broad). Read from the scan of the book at shulmusic.org (Shelf to Shul: Goldfarb, Synagogue Melodies for the High Holydays, 1926, PDF page 9). The fermatas sung as holds: "nu," (and "to" in Baruch shem) held into an added bar, so "A-do-" and "le-o-" stay upbeats; the end of the Shema held into an added bar before Baruch shem; the last "ed." its printed three beats. Breaths written in after "Yisrael," and "Baruch shem," (0.75 beat taken from the note before) and at each fermata. Underlay as the print spaces it: "Sh'ma" one note; "ruch" and "to" each over two notes (sung slurred); the print's two G eighths on "k'-" sung as one G on "ke-". The words respelled from the print's Ashkenazi transliteration ("Sh'ma yisroel", "echod", "Boruch shem k'vod mal'chuso l'olom vo-ed") in modern Israeli pronunciation, the divine names sung in the substituted forms customary when singing outside prayer: Adoshem for the four-letter name, Elokeinu.
